claim: Cytoplasmic accumulation of TDP-43 in motor neurons is the most prominent pathological feature in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
source: Cytoplasmic accumulation of TDP-43 in motor neurons is the most prominent pathological feature in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in ALS research, supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: A feedback cycle between nucleocytoplasmic transport (NCT) defect and TDP-43 aggregation contributes to accumulation of TDP-43 in the cytoplasm.
source: A feedback cycle between nucleocytoplasmic transport (NCT) defect and TDP-43 aggregation was shown to contribute to accumulation of TDP-43 in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Solomon et al., 2018 and Gasset-Rosa et al., 2019 in the manuscript.

claim: Cytosolic calcium is a key cellular factor controlling nucleocytoplasmic transport (NCT) of TDP-43.
source: Here, we identified via FRAP and optogenetics cytosolic calcium as a key cellular factor controlling NCT of TDP-43.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from FRAP and optogenetics experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Dynamic and reversible changes in TDP-43 localization were observed in Drosophila sensory neurons during development.
source: Dynamic and reversible changes in TDP-43 localization were observed in Drosophila sensory neurons during development.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: The cytosolic calcium-Calpain-A-Importin α3 pathway is a regulatory mechanism underlying NCT of TDP-43.
source: Genetic and immunohistochemical analyses identified the cytosolic calcium-Calpain-A-Importin α3 pathway as a regulatory mechanism underlying NCT of TDP-43.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic and immunohistochemical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Upregulation of the calcium-Calpain-A-Importin α3 pathway activity by increasing cytosolic calcium reduced cytoplasmic accumulation of TDP-43 in C9orf72 ALS fly models.
source: In C9orf72 ALS fly models, upregulation of the pathway activity by increasing cytosolic calcium reduced cytoplasmic accumulation of TDP-43 and mitigated behavioral defects.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Upregulation of the calcium-Calpain-A-Importin α3 pathway activity mitigated behavioral defects in C9orf72 ALS fly models.
source: In C9orf72 ALS fly models, upregulation of the pathway activity by increasing cytosolic calcium reduced cytoplasmic accumulation of TDP-43 and mitigated behavioral defects.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and 7D.

claim: Cytoplasmic accumulation of TDP-43 results in impaired protein quality control, mitochondrial dysfunction, and altered stress granule dynamics.
source: Cytoplasmic accumulation of TDP-43 in motor neurons is the most prominent pathological feature in ALS, which results in impaired protein quality control, mitochondrial dysfunction, and altered stress granule dynamics (Shahheydari et al., 2017; Davis et al., 2018; McDonald et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cytoplasmic accumulation of TDP-43 often accompanies depletion of TDP-43 in the nucleus.
source: This cytoplasmic accumulation often accompanies depletion of TDP-43 in the nucleus (Neumann et al., 2006), which then results in the loss of its nuclear functions including mRNA splicing (Highley et al., 2014) and the regulation of transcription (Amlie-Wolf et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Nuclear depletion of TDP-43 results in the loss of its nuclear functions including mRNA splicing and the regulation of transcription.
source: This cytoplasmic accumulation often accompanies depletion of TDP-43 in the nucleus (Neumann et al., 2006), which then results in the loss of its nuclear functions including mRNA splicing (Highley et al., 2014) and the regulation of transcription (Amlie-Wolf et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cytoplasmic accumulation of TDP-43 in neurons is observed in frontotemporal dementia (about 50% of patients).
source: In addition to its occurrence in ALS, the cytoplasmic accumulation of TDP-43 in neurons is also observed in frontotemporal dementia (FTD; about 50% of patients) (Neumann et al., 2006), as well as in Alzheimer's (Amador-Ortiz et al., 2007), Parkinson's (Nakashima-Yasuda et al., 2007), and Huntington's diseases (Schwab et al., 2008), although with lower frequency compared to ALS.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cytoplasmic accumulation of TDP-43 in neurons is observed in Alzheimer's disease.
source: In addition to its occurrence in ALS, the cytoplasmic accumulation of TDP-43 in neurons is also observed in frontotemporal dementia (FTD; about 50% of patients) (Neumann et al., 2006), as well as in Alzheimer's (Amador-Ortiz et al., 2007), Parkinson's (Nakashima-Yasuda et al., 2007), and Huntington's diseases (Schwab et al., 2008), although with lower frequency compared to ALS.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cytoplasmic accumulation of TDP-43 in neurons is observed in Parkinson's disease.
source: In addition to its occurrence in ALS, the cytoplasmic accumulation of TDP-43 in neurons is also observed in frontotemporal dementia (FTD; about 50% of patients) (Neumann et al., 2006), as well as in Alzheimer's (Amador-Ortiz et al., 2007), Parkinson's (Nakashima-Yasuda et al., 2007), and Huntington's diseases (Schwab et al., 2008), although with lower frequency compared to ALS.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cytoplasmic accumulation of TDP-43 in neurons is observed in Huntington's disease.
source: In addition to its occurrence in ALS, the cytoplasmic accumulation of TDP-43 in neurons is also observed in frontotemporal dementia (FTD; about 50% of patients) (Neumann et al., 2006), as well as in Alzheimer's (Amador-Ortiz et al., 2007), Parkinson's (Nakashima-Yasuda et al., 2007), and Huntington's diseases (Schwab et al., 2008), although with lower frequency compared to ALS.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TDP-43 is known to localize mainly in the nucleus of most neurons examined in non-pathological conditions.
source: TDP-43 is known to localize mainly in the nucleus of most neurons examined in non-pathological conditions (Diaper et al., 2013; Neumann et al., 2006; Uchino et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Post-translational modifications (PTMs), such as ubiquitination and phosphorylation, and fragmentation of TDP-43 affect interactions among TDP-43 protein themselves and between TDP-43 and Importins.
source: Post-translational modifications (PTMs), such as ubiquitination and phosphorylation, and fragmentation of TDP-43 were shown to affect interactions among TDP-43 protein themselves and between TDP-43 and Importins, thereby promoting cytoplasmic accumulation of TDP-43 under pathological conditions including ALS (Neumann et al., 2006; Nonaka et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Post-translational modifications (PTMs) and fragmentation of TDP-43 promote cytoplasmic accumulation of TDP-43 under pathological conditions including ALS.
source: Post-translational modifications (PTMs), such as ubiquitination and phosphorylation, and fragmentation of TDP-43 were shown to affect interactions among TDP-43 protein themselves and between TDP-43 and Importins, thereby promoting cytoplasmic accumulation of TDP-43 under pathological conditions including ALS (Neumann et al., 2006; Nonaka et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TDP-43 has a property of shuttling between the nucleus and the cytoplasm in neurons under non-pathological conditions.
source: Of note, TDP-43 has a property of shuttling between the nucleus and the cytoplasm in neurons under non-pathological conditions, and several factors have been shown to contribute to its NCT.
evidence: This is a known property of TDP-43 based on previous research.

claim: Importins (Importin α2, α3, and β1) contribute to nucleocytoplasmic transport of TDP-43.
source: Numerous studies have demonstrated contributions of nuclear transport machineries to NCT of TDP-43, including Importins (Importin α2, α3, and β1) (Nishimura et al., 2010; Solomon et al., 2018), RanGAP (Chou et al., 2018), and components of nuclear pore complexes (Nup62 and Nup54) (Nishimura et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: RanGAP contributes to nucleocytoplasmic transport of TDP-43.
source: Numerous studies have demonstrated contributions of nuclear transport machineries to NCT of TDP-43, including Importins (Importin α2, α3, and β1) (Nishimura et al., 2010; Solomon et al., 2018), RanGAP (Chou et al., 2018), and components of nuclear pore complexes (Nup62 and Nup54) (Nishimura et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Components of nuclear pore complexes (Nup62 and Nup54) contribute to nucleocytoplasmic transport of TDP-43.
source: Numerous studies have demonstrated contributions of nuclear transport machineries to NCT of TDP-43, including Importins (Importin α2, α3, and β1) (Nishimura et al., 2010; Solomon et al., 2018), RanGAP (Chou et al., 2018), and components of nuclear pore complexes (Nup62 and Nup54) (Nishimura et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The nuclear localization signal (NLS) of TDP-43 was first identified in both cultured neurons and mouse brains.
source: The signal sequences for NCT of TDP-43 have been reported: the nuclear localization signal (NLS) of TDP-43 was first identified in both cultured neurons and mouse brains, and its deletion resulted in cytoplasmic accumulation of TDP-43 (Winton et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Winton et al., 2008.

claim: Deletion of the nuclear localization signal (NLS) of TDP-43 resulted in cytoplasmic accumulation of TDP-43.
source: The signal sequences for NCT of TDP-43 have been reported: the nuclear localization signal (NLS) of TDP-43 was first identified in both cultured neurons and mouse brains, and its deletion resulted in cytoplasmic accumulation of TDP-43 (Winton et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Winton et al., 2008.

claim: Deletion of a computationally predicted, leucine-rich nuclear export signal (NES) located at amino acids 239–250 in human TDP-43 showed no significant effects on translocation of TDP-43 towards the cytoplasm in neurons.
source: In contrast, deletion of a computationally predicted, leucine-rich nuclear export signal (NES) located at amino acids 239–250 in human TDP-43 (Winton et al., 2008) showed no significant effects on translocation of TDP-43 towards the cytoplasm in neurons (Pinarbasi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Winton et al., 2008 and Pinarbasi et al., 2018.

claim: C4da neurons showed significantly higher Cyt/Nuc ratios than motor and DA neurons and glial cells by fourfold.
source: C4da neurons showed significantly (p<1.0 × 10−4) higher Cyt/Nuc ratios than motor and DA neurons and glial cells by fourfold (Figure 1A and B), consistent with our hypothesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: TBPH changed its localization from the cytoplasm (120 hr AEL) to the nucleus in the pupal stage at 18 hr after puparium formation (APF).
source: Interestingly, TBPH changed its localization from the cytoplasm (120 hr AEL) to the nucleus in the pupal stage at 18 hr after puparium formation (APF) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: TBPH was localized to both the cytoplasm and the nucleus in an intermediate stage (0 hr APF) between larva and pupa.
source: TBPH was localized to both the cytoplasm and the nucleus in an intermediate stage (0 hr APF) between larva and pupa (Figure 1C), suggesting that TBPH may begin its nuclear entry at this stage.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: TBPH was localized to both the cytoplasm and the nucleus in an early (10 day; 10d) adult stage and then re-localized mainly to the nucleus in the late (40 day; 40d) adult stage.
source: Furthermore, TBPH was localized to both the cytoplasm and the nucleus in an early (10 day; 10d) adult stage and then re-localized mainly to the nucleus in the late (40 day; 40d) adult stage (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cyt/Nuc ratios between pairs of consecutive developmental stages (120 hr AEL-0 hr APF, 0-18 hr APF, 18 hr APF-early adult, and early-late adult) were significantly different.
source: Quantitative comparisons revealed that Cyt/Nuc ratios between pairs of consecutive developmental stages (120 hr AEL-0 hr APF, 0-18 hr APF, 18 hr APF-early adult, and early-late adult) were significantly different (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Endogenous TBPH showed localization patterns similar to—although less dramatic than—overexpressed TBPH.
source: Endogenous TBPH showed localization patterns similar to—although less dramatic than—overexpressed TBPH (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: GCaMP/tdTom mean intensity ratio in pupae was significantly increased compared to that in larvae.
source: GCaMP/tdTom mean intensity ratio in pupae was significantly increased compared to that in larvae (Figure 2B), suggesting that calcium levels have an inverse relationship with Cyt/Nuc ratios of TBPH.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In the Itprka1091/+ pupae, a significantly higher amount of TBPH was localized to the cytoplasm compared to the controls, resulting in an increased Cyt/Nuc ratio.
source: In the Itprka1091/+ pupae, a significantly (p<0.01) higher amount of TBPH was localized to the cytoplasm compared to the controls, resulting in an increased Cyt/Nuc ratio (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Mutation (RyR16/+) of ryanodine receptor led to an increase in the Cyt/Nuc ratio of TBPH.
source: Similarly, mutation (RyR16/+) of ryanodine receptor, another major calcium-releasing channel in the ER, led to a similar increase in the Cyt/Nuc ratio of TBPH (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: In the SERCA Ri larvae, the majority of TBPH was translocated to the nucleus, resulting in a significantly decreased Cyt/Nuc ratio.
source: In the SERCA Ri larvae, the majority of TBPH was translocated to the nucleus, resulting in a significantly (p<1.0 × 10−4) decreased Cyt/Nuc ratio (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: NachBac overexpression led to a decrease in Cyt/Nuc ratio of TBPH.
source: Consistently, NachBac overexpression led to a similar decrease in Cyt/Nuc ratio of TBPH to that in the SERCA Ri larvae (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and G.

claim: Upon optogenetic activation the larvae raised on food containing all trans-retinal (ATR) showed a mild increase (~20%) in intracellular calcium level in C4da neurons expressing channelrhodpsin.
source: We first confirmed that upon optogenetic activation the larvae raised on food containing all trans-retinal (ATR) showed a mild increase (~20%) in intracellular calcium level in C4da neurons expressing channelrhodpsin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H and I; Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H and I.

claim: The Cyt/Nuc ratio of TBPH significantly decreased upon optogenetic stimulation compared to the controls that did not receive any blue light.
source: The Cyt/Nuc ratio of TBPH significantly (p<0.05) decreased compared to the controls that did not receive any blue light (Figure 2H and I).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 2H and I.

claim: A similar decrease in Cyt/Nuc ratio was observed for the RFP-TDP-43 upon optogenetic stimulation.
source: We also expressed RFP-tagged human TDP-43 in C4da neurons and applied the same optogenetics protocol (Figure 2G) before imaging them live. A similar decrease in Cyt/Nuc ratio was observed for the RFP-TDP-43 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J and K) upon optogenetic stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1J and K.

claim: The localization of TDP-43 WT significantly changed from the cytoplasm in larvae to the nucleus in pupae.
source: As expected, the localization of TDP-43 WT significantly changed from the cytoplasm in larvae to the nucleus in pupae (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: The localization of TDP-43 G287S also shifted from the cytoplasm to the nucleus, albeit less so compared to TDP-43 WT.
source: The localization of TDP-43 G287S also shifted from the cytoplasm to the nucleus, albeit less so compared to TDP-43 WT.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: When we decreased cytosolic calcium via ryanodine receptor (RyR) knockdown in pupae, the Cyt/Nuc ratio of TDP-43 WT increased significantly.
source: When we decreased cytosolic calcium via ryanodine receptor (RyR) knockdown in pupae, the Cyt/Nuc ratio of TDP-43 WT increased significantly.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: The localization of TDP-43 G287S also shifted back toward the cytoplasm upon RyR knockdown, but the magnitude of the shift was smaller than that of TDP-43 WT.
source: The localization of TDP-43 G287S also shifted back toward the cytoplasm, but the magnitude of the shift was again smaller than that of TDP-43 WT (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: C4da neurons in larvae that were raised in ATR+ food showed a significantly faster recovery of fluorescence in the nucleus compared to those raised in ATR-.
source: C4da neurons in larvae that were raised in ATR+ food showed a significantly faster (t1/2: 24.9 s; tplateau: 146.3 s; slopemax: 0.01498) recovery of fluorescence in the nucleus compared to those raised in ATR- (t1/2: 46.7 s; tplateau: 200.9 s; slopemax: 0.00528) (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Cytosolic calcium facilitates nuclear import of TBPH in C4da neurons in larvae and pupae.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that cytosolic calcium facilitates nuclear import of TBPH in C4da neurons in larvae and pupae.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the FRAP data and other experimental results.

claim: Knockdown of Calmodulin (Cam), Protein kinase C (Pkc53E), and Calpain-A (CalpA) considerably shifted the localization of TBPH toward the cytoplasm compared to the controls.
source: Among the 12 regulators, knockdown of Calmodulin (Cam), Protein kinase C (Pkc53E), and Calpain-A (CalpA) considerably shifted the localization of TBPH toward the cytoplasm compared to the controls (Figure 4B), thereby significantly (p<0.05) increasing Cyt/Nuc ratios (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Knockdown of Importin alpha 1 (Imp α1), Importin alpha 3 (Imp α3), Importin beta 1 (Imp β1), Importin 7 (Imp 7), and Transportin-Serine/Arginine rich (Tnpo-SR) considerably shifted the localization of TBPH toward the cytoplasm.
source: Among the 12 components, knockdown of Importin alpha 1 (Imp α1), Importin alpha 3 (Imp α3), Importin beta 1 (Imp β1), Importin 7 (Imp 7), and Transportin-Serine/Arginine rich (Tnpo-SR) considerably shifted the localization of TBPH toward the cytoplasm (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) and significantly increased Cyt/Nuc ratios (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Overexpression of Imp α3, Imp β1, or Imp α3 and Imp β1 shifted the localization of TBPH from the cytoplasm to the nucleus.
source: Consistent with the findings from knockdown experiments, overexpression of Imp α3 (Imp α3 O/E), Imp β1 (Imp β1 O/E), or Imp α3 and Imp β1 (Imp α3 O/E + Imp β1 O/E) shifted the localization of TBPH from the cytoplasm to the nucleus (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Co-overexpression of CalpA increased the amount of Imp α3 in the nucleus compared to the controls, and significantly decreased the Cyt/Nuc ratio of Imp α3.
source: Co-overexpression of CalpA, however, increased the amount of Imp α3 in the nucleus compared to the controls, and significantly (p<1.0 × 10−3) decreased the Cyt/Nuc ratio of Imp α3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Knockdown of CalpA significantly shifted the localization of Imp α3 toward the cytoplasm compared to the controls, thereby increasing the Cyt/Nuc ratio of Imp α3.
source: Knockdown of CalpA significantly shifted the localization of Imp α3 toward the cytoplasm compared to the controls, thereby increasing the Cyt/Nuc ratio of Imp α3 (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Knockdown of SERCA significantly decreased Cyt/Nuc ratio of Imp α3.
source: Knockdown of SERCA, which increases the amount of cytosolic calcium, also significantly (p<0.05) decreased Cyt/Nuc ratio of Imp α3 (Figure 5C and D), similar to CalpA co-overexpression.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: In C4da neurons co-overexpressing SERCA Ri and CalpA Ri, Imp α3 was predominantly localized in the cytoplasm, implying that the effect of SERCA knockdown was abolished by the CalpA knockdown.
source: In these C4da neurons, Imp α3 was predominantly localized in the cytoplasm, implying that the effect of SERCA knockdown was abolished by the CalpA knockdown (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Co-overexpression of SERCA Ri and Imp α3 Ri reversed the TBPH localization from the nucleus to the cytoplasm.
source: However, co-overexpression of SERCA Ri and Imp α3 Ri (SERCA Ri + Imp α3 Ri) reversed the TBPH localization from the nucleus to the cytoplasm (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: C4da neurons expressing TDP-43 showed more aberrant dendrite arborization pattern compared to those expressing TDP-43-ΔNLS.
source: Interestingly, we found that C4da neurons expressing TDP-43 showed more aberrant dendrite arborization pattern compared to those expressing TDP-43-ΔNLS (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: C4da neurons expressing TDP-43 exhibited significantly shorter total dendritic length compared to those expressing TDP-43-ΔNLS.
source: Further analysis showed that C4da neurons expressing TDP-43 exhibited significantly shorter total dendritic length (Figure 6B) and fewer number of dendritic branch points compared to those expressing TDP-43-ΔNLS (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: C4da neurons expressing TDP-43 exhibited fewer number of dendritic branch points compared to those expressing TDP-43-ΔNLS.
source: Further analysis showed that C4da neurons expressing TDP-43 exhibited significantly shorter total dendritic length (Figure 6B) and fewer number of dendritic branch points compared to those expressing TDP-43-ΔNLS (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The complexity of dendritic arbor in C4da neurons expressing TDP-43 was significantly reduced compared to those expressing TDP-43-ΔNLS and controls.
source: Also, sholl analysis indicated that the complexity of dendritic arbor in C4da neurons expressing TDP-43 was significantly reduced compared to those expressing TDP-43-ΔNLS and controls (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Sholl analysis data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: SERCA knockdown decreased the total dendritic length in larval C4da neurons.
source: SERCA knockdown, which promotes nuclear translocation of overexpressed TBPH, decreased the total dendritic length (Figure 6E and F) and the number of dendritic branch points (Figure 6E and G) in larval C4da neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: SERCA knockdown decreased the number of dendritic branch points in larval C4da neurons.
source: SERCA knockdown, which promotes nuclear translocation of overexpressed TBPH, decreased the total dendritic length (Figure 6E and F) and the number of dendritic branch points (Figure 6E and G) in larval C4da neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 6E and G.

claim: Itpr knockdown increased the total dendritic length and the number of dendritic branch points.
source: Itpr knockdown (Figure 6E and G) or mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–1C), which inhibit nuclear translocation of overexpressed TBPH, increased the total dendritic length and the number of dendritic branch points.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 6E, G, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–1C.

claim: Overexpression of Imp α3 significantly decreased the total dendritic lengths of C4da neurons overexpressing TBPH.
source: Moreover, overexpression and knockdown of Imp α3 significantly decreased and increased, respectively, the total dendritic lengths (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and E) and the number of dendritic branch points (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and F) of C4da neurons overexpressing TBPH.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: Knockdown of Imp α3 significantly increased the total dendritic lengths of C4da neurons overexpressing TBPH.
source: Moreover, overexpression and knockdown of Imp α3 significantly decreased and increased, respectively, the total dendritic lengths (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and E) and the number of dendritic branch points (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and F) of C4da neurons overexpressing TBPH.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: Overexpression of Imp α3 significantly decreased the number of dendritic branch points of C4da neurons overexpressing TBPH.
source: Moreover, overexpression and knockdown of Imp α3 significantly decreased and increased, respectively, the total dendritic lengths (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and E) and the number of dendritic branch points (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and F) of C4da neurons overexpressing TBPH.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and F.

claim: Knockdown of Imp α3 significantly increased the number of dendritic branch points of C4da neurons overexpressing TBPH.
source: Moreover, overexpression and knockdown of Imp α3 significantly decreased and increased, respectively, the total dendritic lengths (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and E) and the number of dendritic branch points (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and F) of C4da neurons overexpressing TBPH.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and F.

claim: Imp α3 Ri significantly increased the dendritic complexity of TBPH O/E.
source: Furthermore, Imp α3 Ri significantly increased the dendritic complexity of TBPH O/E, whereas Imp α3 O/E decreased the complexity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by Sholl analysis data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Imp α3 O/E decreased the dendritic complexity of TBPH O/E.
source: Furthermore, Imp α3 Ri significantly increased the dendritic complexity of TBPH O/E, whereas Imp α3 O/E decreased the complexity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by Sholl analysis data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The Cyt/Nuc ratio of TBPH was increased in the PR100- and GR100-expressing larval motor neurons compared to in the control.
source: We first confirmed that the Cyt/Nuc ratio of TBPH was increased in the PR100- and GR100-expressing larval motor neurons (Figure 7A left panels and 7B), compared to in the control (Ctrl), consistent with previous observation in adult fly brains (Solomon et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: Increased cytosolic calcium restored the Cyt/Nuc ratio of TBPH significantly in the PR100- and GR100-expressing larval motor neurons.
source: Increased cytosolic calcium restored the Cyt/Nuc ratio of TBPH significantly (p<0.05) in the PR100- and GR100-expressing larval motor neurons (Figure 7A right panels and 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: Larvae overexpressing GR100 showed a significant decrease in the distance travelled compared to the controls.
source: After repeating the experiments using more than 23 different larvae for each genotype, we found that larvae overexpressing SERCA Ri showed no significant change in the distance travelled compared to the controls, whereas those overexpressing GR100 showed a significant (p<0.05) decrease compared to the controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The larvae co-overexpressing GR100 and SERCA Ri travelled a longer distance than those expressing only GR100.
source: The larvae co-overexpressing GR100 and SERCA Ri travelled a longer distance than those expressing only GR100 (Figure 7D), indicating mitigation of larval locomotion defect.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The calcium-CalpA-Imp α3 pathway is likely to precede the sequestration of Importins by cytoplasmic TDP-43 aggregates and the subsequent NCT defects in the feedback cycle model.
source: Given this observation, the calcium-CalpA-Imp α3 pathway is likely to precede the sequestration of Importins by cytoplasmic TDP-43 aggregates and the subsequent NCT defects in the feedback cycle model.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that TDP-43 aggregates were not observed in the study.

claim: A reduction in CalpA mitigated polyQ-induced retinal degeneration.
source: Notably, a reduction in CalpA mitigated polyQ-induced retinal degeneration (Figure 7—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3B.

claim: CalpA overexpression led to no apparent pattern of TBPH cleavage on the blot.
source: We found that CalpA overexpression led to no apparent pattern of TBPH cleavage on the blot (Figure 7—figure supplement 4A and B), although unexpectedly, it led to an increase in the amount of TBPH.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4A and B.

claim: CalpA overexpression led to an increase in the amount of TBPH.
source: We found that CalpA overexpression led to no apparent pattern of TBPH cleavage on the blot (Figure 7—figure supplement 4A and B), although unexpectedly, it led to an increase in the amount of TBPH.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4A and B.

claim: CalpA is necessary for nuclear import of TBPH.
source: Instead, we showed that CalpA is necessary for nuclear import of TBPH (Figure 4B and C) through a yet undefined mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Importin α3, a human orthologue of Imp α3, has not been reported as a substrate of Calpain, nor predicted using the Calpain cleavage detector (CCD) software.
source: However, Importin α3, a human orthologue of Imp α3, has not been reported as a substrate of Calpain, nor predicted using the Calpain cleavage detector (CCD) software (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is based on a literature search and computational prediction.

claim: Imp α3/β1 complex is the major transport regulator for nuclear import of TBPH.
